pamphlet_excerpts: Rockfall Protection: Climbers and belayers must wear approved helmets within active crag rockfall zones.
Anchor Redundancy: Multi-point anchors require independent load distribution to survive a single component failure.
Hypothermia Prevention: Wet climbing clothing accelerates rapid core cooling even during warm summer ascents.
Lightning Protocol: High crag exposure requires immediate descent when thunder clouds approach the area.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Perimeter Check: Survey the crag cliff base to identify loose rock and drainage hazards.
Step 2 - Safe Zone Setup: Designate a protected gear staging and resting location outside falling rock zones.
Step 3 - First Aid Prep: Place an accessible first aid kit near the staging ground before climbing.
Step 4 - Hazard Briefing: Review rockfall warning calls, weather retreat routes, and evacuation tasks with partners.

pamphlet_excerpts: Durable Surfaces: Travel on established trails to preserve sensitive vegetation growing around cliff bases.
Waste Removal: Pack out all athletic tape, food scraps, and solid personal sanitary waste.
Natural State: Leave natural rocks, plants, and historical artifacts undisturbed for other crag visitors.
Respect Wildlife: Avoid disturbing nesting cliff birds during designated springtime nesting restriction periods.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Trail Travel: Walk exclusively along marked trails when approaching the designated rock cliff base.
Step 2 - Staging Placement: Position backpacks and gear on durable flat rocks rather than fragile vegetation.
Step 3 - Chalk Cleanup: Brush excess chalk residue from holds before packing equipment at day end.
Step 4 - Waste Sweep: Collect every stray wrapper, tape scrap, and gear strand before departing.

pamphlet_excerpts: Snug Fit: Wear form-fitting athletic layers that cannot catch inside active belay friction hardware.
Hair Restraint: Tie long hair securely back against the head to avoid moving gear.
Jewelry Removal: Remove all rings, necklaces, and wristwatches before touching climbing ropes or hardware.
Weather Shells: Pack breathable, water-resistant outer layers to withstand sudden temperature drops at crags.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Jewelry Removal: Take off all rings, necklaces, bracelets, and watches before putting on gear.
Step 2 - Hair Securing: Fasten long hair tightly behind the neck using a clean elastic band.
Step 3 - Garment Tucking: Tuck loose shirts and waist drawstrings completely inside the climbing harness waistbelt.
Step 4 - Footwear Lacing: Tie climbing shoes securely to prevent foot slippage on small rock edges.

pamphlet_excerpts: Name Inclusion: State your partner name before shouting commands to prevent cross-wall communication errors.
Belay Confirmation: Wait for the belayer to respond with belay on before climbing.
Tension Requests: Shout tension clearly when needing the belayer to remove all rope slack.
Rockfall Alarm: Shout rock loudly and instantly whenever any object falls down the cliff.

Step 3 - Climb Announcement: State climbing clearly before placing hands and feet onto the rock face.
Step 4 - Climb Permission: Begin ascending only after hearing the belayer confirm with climb on.

left_points: (5a) Climber Standard Verbal Commands: Climbers communicate their ascent status using distinct calls like climbing, slack, and up rope. They must await direct verbal acknowledgment from the belayer before moving.

(5b) Rappeller Descent Voice Signals: Rappellers confirm their descending system and belay backup using clear commands like on rappel. They signal off rappel only after clearing the landing zone completely.
right_points: (5c) Belayer Verbal Safety Responses: Belayers maintain vigilant voice contact, responding promptly to requests for slack or tension. They confirm readiness only when their brake hand securely controls the rope.

left_points: (6a) Climbing Rope Type Standards: Climbing requires certified dynamic kernmantle ropes designed to absorb fall forces through controlled elongation. Static ropes are reserved exclusively for hauling gear and fixed-line rappelling.

(6b) Rope Physical Wear Examination: Rope examination combines visual scanning for sheath cuts with tactile pinching to find core gaps. Any exposed inner core fibers or flat deformities require taking the rope out of service.
right_points: (6c) Rope Damage Prevention Methods: Climbers protect ropes by using protective tarps, padding sharp rock edges, and avoiding foot traffic. Clean storage away from sunlight, heat, and corrosive chemicals extends rope lifespan.

(6d) Rope Retirement Decision Criteria: Retiring a rope is mandatory after severe high-impact falls, chemical contamination, or excessive sheath abrasion. Cut retired ropes into short utility lengths to prevent accidental life-safety reuse.

left_points: (7a) Figure Eight Bight Knot: The figure eight on a bight creates a strong, reliable loop in the end or middle of a rope. It resists slipping and remains relatively easy to untie after holding a climber weight.

(7b) Figure Eight Follow-Through Tie-In: The figure eight follow-through is the universal standard for tying a climbing rope directly into a harness. Its symmetrical pattern makes visual inspection straightforward for both climber and belayer.
right_points: (7c) Water Knot Webbing Splice: The water knot joins flat nylon webbing into runners and sling anchors by retracing an overhand knot. Climbers must leave substantial tails and check them frequently for movement.

(7d) Double Fisherman Joining Knot: The double fisherman knot joins two ropes together for multi-pitch rappels or creates closed cord loops for Prusik hitches. Its interlocking structure tightens under load to prevent accidental release.

rows.left: (7a) Figure Eight on a Bight: For tying together the ends of two ropes, the most reliable knot is the double fisherman's knot (p. 53).
rows.right: (7c) Water Knot for Webbing: Half of a double fisherman's knot (also known as a barrel knot) can be used as a stopper knot at the end of a rope (p. 53).

rows.left: (7b) Figure Eight Follow-Through Knot: It can also be used to secure the ends of a piece of cord to form a runner (p. 53).
rows.right: (7d) Double Fisherman's Grapevine Knot: Lay about 2 feet of the ends of two ropes alongside one another, ends opposite (p. 53).

rows.left: Barrel Stopper Knot: Half of a double fisherman's knot (also known as a barrel knot) can be used as a stopper knot at the end of a rope (p. 53).
rows.right: (7e) Prusik Hitch on a Rope: For tying together the ends of two ropes, the most reliable knot is the double fisherman's knot (p. 53).

Harness Inspection: Confirm waistbelts rest above hips with all buckles doubled back securely.

pamphlet_excerpts: Brake Hand Rule: The brake hand must never leave the brake strand of the climbing rope.
PBUS Method: Use Pull, Brake, Under, Slide movements to manage rope slack without releasing control.
Backup Redundancy: Backup belayers hold the brake rope to stop falls if belayers fail.
Weight Disparity: Anchor the belayer to the ground when the climber outweighs them significantly.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Rigging Belay: Thread the rope bight through the belay device and lock the carabiner.
Step 2 - Stance Positioning: Establish an athletic braced stance facing the rock face with brake hand down.
Step 3 - PBUS Cycling: Pull rope, brake downward, place guide hand under, and slide upward smoothly.
Step 4 - Fall Arrest: Lock the brake strand firmly downward across the device when catching falls.

requirements.pamphlet_summary: Proper climbing equipment storage preserves the structural integrity of synthetic nylon fibers and metal hardware. Ropes, harnesses, and hardware must be kept clean, dry, and shielded from corrosive chemicals.
socratic_questions: Why does sulfuric acid vapor destroy nylon webbing without leaving obvious visual signs?
How does storing wet ropes inside airtight plastic containers cause mold and rot?
What inspection steps should you take before using gear that sat in storage?

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Under BSA's 'Climb On Safely' guidelines in Climbing Requirement 1, what must the climber and belayer verify during their verbal and visual buddy check before the climber leaves the ground?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Under BSA's 'Climb On Safely' guidelines in Climbing Requirement 1, what must the climber and belayer verify during their verbal and visual buddy check before the climber leaves the ground?
options: A. That the climber's harness waist belt hangs loosely below the hip bones and the rope is clipped with a single non-locking accessory carabiner.

B. That UIAA/ASTM climbing helmets are fastened, harnesses are doubled-back/properly buckled snug above the hips, the climber's figure-eight follow-through knot with safety backup is tied through the correct tie-in loops, and the belay device and locking carabiner are threaded and locked.
C. That the belayer is wearing slick leather gardening gloves and standing thirty feet back from the base of the cliff while looking at a phone.
D. That the climbing rope is tied directly around the climber's bare waist with a square knot and anchored to a single dry bush at the cliff edge.
choices: A. That the climber's harness waist belt hangs loosely below the hip bones and the rope is clipped with a single non-locking accessory carabiner.

B. That UIAA/ASTM climbing helmets are fastened, harnesses are doubled-back/properly buckled snug above the hips, the climber's figure-eight follow-through knot with safety backup is tied through the correct tie-in loops, and the belay device and locking carabiner are threaded and locked.
C. That the belayer is wearing slick leather gardening gloves and standing thirty feet back from the base of the cliff while looking at a phone.
D. That the climbing rope is tied directly around the climber's bare waist with a square knot and anchored to a single dry bush at the cliff edge.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. That UIAA/ASTM climbing helmets are fastened, harnesses are doubled-back/properly buckled snug above the hips, the climber's figure-eight follow-through knot with safety backup is tied through the correct tie-in loops, and the belay device and locking carabiner are threaded and locked.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Climb On Safely requires certified climbing helmets, properly fitted and buckled harnesses, a correctly tied figure-eight follow-through knot, a properly threaded belay device with a locked carabiner, and standardized verbal commands before climbing.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What should a unit do if a Scout becomes unusually fearful and refuses to step over the edge for a rappel?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What should a unit do if a Scout becomes unusually fearful and refuses to step over the edge for a rappel?
options: A. Have two older Scouts guide the hesitant Scout over the edge
B. Respect the decision and never force or pressure anyone to participate
C. Require the Scout to complete at least half the rappel to earn credit
D. Remove the backup belay so the rope moves faster through the device
choices: A. Have two older Scouts guide the hesitant Scout over the edge
B. Respect the decision and never force or pressure anyone to participate
C. Require the Scout to complete at least half the rappel to earn credit
D. Remove the backup belay so the rope moves faster through the device
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Respect the decision and never force or pressure anyone to participate
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Climb Safely guidelines state that no one should ever be forced or pressured into doing an activity with which they are uncomfortable (p. 9).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why must climbers tuck in loose shirts, secure long hair, and avoid clothing with drawstrings before rappelling?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why must climbers tuck in loose shirts, secure long hair, and avoid clothing with drawstrings before rappelling?
options: A. Drawstrings, hair, and baggy clothing can get caught in a belay or rappel device
B. Loose fabric absorbs moisture and makes the rope heavier
C. Brightly colored loose shirts distract the spotter on the ground
D. Extra fabric increases wind resistance when descending a steep face
choices: A. Drawstrings, hair, and baggy clothing can get caught in a belay or rappel device
B. Loose fabric absorbs moisture and makes the rope heavier
C. Brightly colored loose shirts distract the spotter on the ground
D. Extra fabric increases wind resistance when descending a steep face
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Drawstrings, hair, and baggy clothing can get caught in a belay or rappel device
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Proper climbing attire must be entanglement-free so hair, drawstrings, and loose fabric cannot jam inside belay or rappel devices (p. 90).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does top-rope climbing differ from lead climbing on a vertical rock face?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does top-rope climbing differ from lead climbing on a vertical rock face?
options: A. Top-rope climbers ascend without a harness while spotters stand below
B. Top-rope climbers are protected by a rope running through an anchor already set at the top of the route
C. Top-rope climbers clip the rope into protection wedges as they ascend
D. Top-rope climbers use static rope to prevent stretching during a fall
choices: A. Top-rope climbers ascend without a harness while spotters stand below
B. Top-rope climbers are protected by a rope running through an anchor already set at the top of the route
C. Top-rope climbers clip the rope into protection wedges as they ascend
D. Top-rope climbers use static rope to prevent stretching during a fall
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Top-rope climbers are protected by a rope running through an anchor already set at the top of the route
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): In top-rope climbing, the belay rope passes through a secure anchor at the top of the climb, catching the climber immediately with minimal fall distance (p. 36).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: During a climb, which verbal command tells the belayer to pull in loose rope and hold the climber firmly?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: During a climb, which verbal command tells the belayer to pull in loose rope and hold the climber firmly?
options: A. Slack
B. Off belay
C. Up rope or Tension
D. Climb on
choices: A. Slack
B. Off belay
C. Up rope or Tension
D. Climb on
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Calling 'Up rope' tells the belayer to pull in any loose slack, and 'Tension' instructs the belayer to pull the rope tight and lock off to support the climber (p. 66).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What indicates that a kernmantle rope must be retired immediately during a pre-climb inspection?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What indicates that a kernmantle rope must be retired immediately during a pre-climb inspection?
options: A. The rope feels slightly stiff after being coiled in a dry closet
B. The middle marker tape on the sheath has faded from washing in mild soap
C. The rope has been used for three top-rope climbs on an indoor wall
D. The white inner core fibers are visible through a torn sheath or you feel a soft flat spot
choices: A. The rope feels slightly stiff after being coiled in a dry closet
B. The middle marker tape on the sheath has faded from washing in mild soap
C. The rope has been used for three top-rope climbs on an indoor wall
D. The white inner core fibers are visible through a torn sheath or you feel a soft flat spot
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. The white inner core fibers are visible through a torn sheath or you feel a soft flat spot
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Exposed inner core fibers, soft or flat spots, hard lumps, or chemical contamination mean the kernmantle rope's integrity is compromised and it must be retired immediately (p. 46).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which knot is specifically designed for tying two ends of tubular webbing together to form a runner?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which knot is specifically designed for tying two ends of tubular webbing together to form a runner?
options: A. Figure eight on a bight
B. Water knot
C. Prusik hitch
D. Double fisherman's knot
choices: A. Figure eight on a bight
B. Water knot
C. Prusik hitch
D. Double fisherman's knot
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): The water knot traces an overhand knot in reverse with the opposing end of webbing, sitting flat and holding securely in tubular webbing (p. 52).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How can you verify that the adjustable leg loops on your climbing harness are tightened to the proper tension?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How can you verify that the adjustable leg loops on your climbing harness are tightened to the proper tension?
options: A. You should just be able to slip two fingers between the loop and your thigh
B. You should be able to fit your entire fist between the strap and your leg
C. The leg loops should hang loosely at least two inches below your thigh
D. The straps should be tight enough to leave a red indentation before climbing
choices: A. You should just be able to slip two fingers between the loop and your thigh
B. You should be able to fit your entire fist between the strap and your leg
C. The leg loops should hang loosely at least two inches below your thigh
D. The straps should be tight enough to leave a red indentation before climbing
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. You should just be able to slip two fingers between the loop and your thigh
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Slipping just two fingers between the leg loop and your thigh confirms the harness is snug enough for safety without cutting off blood circulation (p. 57).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What do the five letters of the Scouting America pre-climb CHECK system stand for?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What do the five letters of the Scouting America pre-climb CHECK system stand for?
options: A. Climber, Helmet, Environment, Cord, Knots
B. Carabiner, Hitch, Emergency, Communication, Kernmantle
C. Clothing, Harness, Equipment, Carabiners, Knots
D. Checkpoints, Holds, Edges, Crags, Karabiners
choices: A. Climber, Helmet, Environment, Cord, Knots
B. Carabiner, Hitch, Emergency, Communication, Kernmantle
C. Clothing, Harness, Equipment, Carabiners, Knots
D. Checkpoints, Holds, Edges, Crags, Karabiners
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Clothing, Harness, Equipment, Carabiners, Knots
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): The CHECK acronym reminds climbers and belayers to inspect Clothing, Harness, Equipment, Carabiners, and Knots before leaving the ground or cliff edge (p. 60).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What is the number one rule for the brake hand while belaying a climber or rappeller?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the number one rule for the brake hand while belaying a climber or rappeller?
options: A. Keep the brake hand above the belay device to feed slack faster
B. Never let go of the brake strand with the brake hand while someone is on belay
C. Switch brake hands after every five feet of rope movement
D. Wrap the brake strand twice around your wrist for extra grip
choices: A. Keep the brake hand above the belay device to feed slack faster
B. Never let go of the brake strand with the brake hand while someone is on belay
C. Switch brake hands after every five feet of rope movement
D. Wrap the brake strand twice around your wrist for extra grip
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Never let go of the brake strand with the brake hand while someone is on belay
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Friction in a belay device depends entirely on the brake hand controlling the free end of the rope, so the brake hand must never leave the rope (p. 64).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why should you keep your weight over your feet rather than hugging the rock face with your chest while climbing?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why should you keep your weight over your feet rather than hugging the rock face with your chest while climbing?
options: A. It keeps chalk dust off your shirt and harness
B. It allows the belayer to see your tie-in knot from the ground
C. It prevents the climbing rope from touching the rock surface
D. It presses your climbing shoes firmly onto footholds and lets your strong leg muscles lift your weight
choices: A. It keeps chalk dust off your shirt and harness
B. It allows the belayer to see your tie-in knot from the ground
C. It prevents the climbing rope from touching the rock surface
D. It presses your climbing shoes firmly onto footholds and lets your strong leg muscles lift your weight
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. It presses your climbing shoes firmly onto footholds and lets your strong leg muscles lift your weight
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Keeping your weight centered over your feet maximizes shoe friction on holds and uses strong leg muscles instead of tiring your arms (p. 70).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What is the proper body posture when walking backward down a cliff face on rappel?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the proper body posture when walking backward down a cliff face on rappel?
options: A. Lean forward with your chest against the rock and tiptoe down
B. Lean back with feet shoulder-width apart and flat against the wall, weight on your heels
C. Push off forcefully with both legs to clear ten feet at a time
D. Hold both hands above the rappel device to support your upper body
choices: A. Lean forward with your chest against the rock and tiptoe down
B. Lean back with feet shoulder-width apart and flat against the wall, weight on your heels
C. Push off forcefully with both legs to clear ten feet at a time
D. Hold both hands above the rappel device to support your upper body
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Lean back with feet shoulder-width apart and flat against the wall, weight on your heels
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Leaning back into the harness with feet shoulder-width apart, flat against the face, and weight on your heels provides stability and smooth control (p. 60).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Where should coiled climbing ropes, harnesses, and webbing be stored between outings?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Where should coiled climbing ropes, harnesses, and webbing be stored between outings?
options: A. In the trunk of a car alongside spare motor oil and a car battery
B. Hung on a sunny porch wall where ultraviolet light prevents mildew
C. In a clean, cool, dry, and dark place away from sunlight, heat, and all chemicals
D. Sealed tightly inside an airtight plastic bag while still damp from rain
choices: A. In the trunk of a car alongside spare motor oil and a car battery
B. Hung on a sunny porch wall where ultraviolet light prevents mildew
C. In a clean, cool, dry, and dark place away from sunlight, heat, and all chemicals
D. Sealed tightly inside an airtight plastic bag while still damp from rain
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. In a clean, cool, dry, and dark place away from sunlight, heat, and all chemicals
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Nylon ropes, harnesses, and webbing must be dried thoroughly in the shade and stored in a cool, dark, dry location away from sunlight, heat, and chemicals (p. 47).
